title: Strategic Verification for Long-Running LLM Agents
content: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-turn text generators into long- 2 running systems capable of multi-step reasoning, tool use, persistent memory, and reusable 3 skill development. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve 4 agent reliability, but existing approaches commonly treat verification as a fixed component 5 of the reward structure, creating challenges related to sparse credit assignment, verifier 6 reliability, reward hacking, path compliance, and verification cost. We introduce Budgeted 7 Adaptive Verification with Asymmetric Rewards (BAVAR), a framework that formulates 8 verification as a sequential, resource-constrained decision problem. BAVAR selectively 9 determines what to verify, when verification is valuable, which verifier to invoke, and how 10 verified evidence should influence learning based on uncertainty, action criticality, verifier 11 reliability, expected verification value, and remaining computational budget. It combines 12 reliability-gated positive process rewards with persistent penalties for path violations and 13 extends verification to persistent memories and reusable skills. We evaluate BAVAR in 14 two studies. In a simulation study under matched budgets, BAVAR outperformed uniform 15 dense verification when verification was scarce (62.2% vs. 54.8% safe verified success), 16 showed an estimated advantage of 2.8 percentage points at a medium budget (74.7% vs. 17 71.9%) that was not significant after Holm correction; it reduced severe path violations and 18 achieved the highest promotion precision (94.4%) for persistent artifacts, with ablations 19 attributing these gains mainly to asymmetric rewards and lifecycle gates. In a preregistered 20 runtime experiment on a campus-information agent (77 tasks, 2310 episodes, real model 21 calls), verification reduced safety violations from 9.5% to 0.9% of episodes; BAVAR matched 22 dense verification’s correct-and-safe rate (91.3%) while using 77% fewer judge calls and 23 about one-third of the median latency. In both studies, the value of verification was limited 24 less by detecting errors than by recovering from them. These findings suggest that adaptive 25 verification is most useful when verification is scarce or costly, and they motivate evaluation 26 on public benchmarks and with reinforcement-learning training of real agents.
